opus-5.5.text:
I think they're deeply related, and in many ways robotics foundation models are standing on the shoulders of large language models. If you look at how the field has evolved over the last few years, a lot of the breakthroughs in robotics came from borrowing the recipe that worked so well for language: take a very large, general model, train it on huge amounts of diverse data, and let general capabilities emerge, rather than hand-engineering a separate solution for every single task.

Concretely, many of the robotics models today, the vision-language-action models, actually start from a pretrained vision-language model. The robot inherits a lot of common sense and semantic understanding from internet-scale data. It knows what an apple is, what "put the trash away" means, which object is the one that looks like a dinosaur, without ever having seen that in robot data. Then we fine-tune it so that, in addition to outputting words, it can output actions. So in a sense, actions become just another kind of language the model learns to speak.

But I'd also emphasize the differences, because I think that's where the real research challenges are. The biggest one is data. Language models had the internet, trillions of tokens essentially sitting there for free. Robotics has no such thing. Every piece of robot data has to be collected in the physical world, through teleoperation or real deployments, and that's slow and expensive. So the scaling laws that worked so cleanly for LLMs are much harder to realize in robotics. A lot of our effort goes into figuring out how to get more data, whether through simulation, learning from human videos, cross-embodiment data from many different robots, or having robots improve themselves.

The second difference is that the physical world is unforgiving. If a language model makes a mistake, you get a wrong sentence and you can regenerate it. If a robot makes a mistake, it might drop a glass or bump into a person. Real-time control, safety, and precision in contact-rich manipulation are things language never had to deal with. There's also the question of embodiment: the same intelligence has to work through very different bodies, arms, grippers, humanoids, each with its own physics.

So my view is that the paradigm is converging. The core philosophy of generality and scale is shared, and I believe robotics will eventually have its own "GPT moment." But we can't simply copy and paste. We have to solve the data problem and the physical grounding problem that are unique to embodied intelligence. And interestingly, I think it will go both ways. Robotics may eventually give back to language models, because an intelligence that truly understands the physical world through interaction is something that pure text alone may never fully capture.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics models often start from pretrained vision-language models and are fine-tuned to output actions. It describes borrowing the LLM recipe, but does not clearly characterize development as adapting existing large language models themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I actually moved from working on locomotion and sim-to-real into the foundation model space, and the two paradigms feel both deeply connected and fundamentally different.

The connection is pretty clear. The language model story taught everyone the same lesson: if you have a general architecture, a simple objective, and you scale data and compute together, you get capabilities that no amount of hand-engineering would have produced. In robotics, that lesson translated into things like RT-1, RT-2, and the vision-language-action models that followed. We stopped building one policy per task per robot and started asking, can a single model control many embodiments across many tasks, and does it keep improving as you feed it more. The answer so far seems to be yes, and that reframing is the biggest thing robotics borrowed from the language world.

But the differences matter just as much. The first is data. Language models had the internet sitting there, essentially free. Robotics has no equivalent. Every trajectory with real actions has to be collected, either by teleoperation, which is expensive and slow, or in simulation, where you then pay the sim-to-real tax, or from videos of humans, where the action labels are missing. So a large portion of robotics research is really about the data problem, not the model problem. How do you make data collection cheaper, how do you cross embodiments so data from one robot helps another, how do you squeeze knowledge out of internet video that was never meant for robots.

The second difference is the nature of the output. Text tokens are discrete and the world does not push back when you generate them. A robot acts in continuous time, in a physical world, with latency, noise, contact dynamics, and real consequences if it is wrong. That means the control side still matters enormously. A lot of us learned over years of locomotion work that the last few percent of robustness comes from things like reinforcement learning fine-tuning, good low-level controllers, and careful handling of physics. Pretraining gives you common sense about the world, but it does not automatically give you the reflexes.

The third difference is evaluation. In language, you can run a benchmark overnight. In robotics, evaluating a policy means someone standing next to a real robot for days, and the results depend on lighting, object placement, wear on the hardware. This slows down the whole research loop, and I think it is one of the underappreciated reasons the field moves at a different pace.

So my overall view is that robotics foundation models are following the spirit of the language model paradigm, with the insistence on generality and scale, but they cannot simply copy the recipe. The really interesting research right now lives exactly at that gap, where you take the pretrained understanding from large models and marry it with the physical grounding that only comes from acting in the world. I do not think either one alone gets us to robots that are genuinely useful in people's homes. It is the combination.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics borrowed the language-model paradigm and combines pretrained understanding with physical grounding, but it does not characterize current robotics foundation-model development as adapting existing LLMs.

astra-6.text:
我觉得这两个方向在研究范式上有很强的共通性。大语言模型给我们的一个启发是，可以先用大规模、多样化的数据训练一个通用模型，再让它适应不同的任务。机器人基础模型也希望做到这一点：不再为每一个任务单独开发一套系统，而是让同一个模型能够完成多种任务，并且把学到的能力迁移到新的环境中。

但机器人不是简单地把大语言模型接到一个机械臂上。语言模型主要处理文本，而机器人要把视觉、语言和动作联系起来，还要在真实世界里形成闭环。比如你让机器人拿起一个杯子，它不仅要理解“杯子”是什么，还要判断杯子在哪里、应该怎么抓，以及碰到杯子以后怎么调整动作。理解任务和可靠地完成任务，是两个不同的层次。

另一个很大的区别是数据。互联网提供了大量现成的文本，但机器人交互数据往往需要实际操作才能获得，成本高，而且不同机器人之间的数据也不容易直接通用。所以机器人能借鉴大语言模型的预训练和规模化思路，但如何收集数据、如何利用仿真、如何从交互中学习，都需要自己的方法。

所以我的看法是，两者会越来越多地融合，但不一定沿着完全相同的路径发展。语言模型可以提供知识和任务理解，而机器人研究还需要解决物理交互、动作控制和可靠性的问题。最终我们关心的是，模型能不能把它所理解的东西，变成真实世界里有效的行动。

r001.rationale: The response says robotics can borrow large language models’ pretraining and scaling ideas and may use language models for knowledge and task understanding. It does not characterize current robotics foundation-model development as adapting existing LLMs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the two paradigms are closely related, but robotics adds some important challenges. With large language models, we’ve seen how training a general model on broad data can create a foundation for many different tasks. Robotics foundation models pursue a similar idea: instead of building a separate system for every task, can we train a model that transfers across tasks, environments, and perhaps even different robots?

The biggest difference is the data. Language has an enormous amount of text available on the internet. In robotics, we need data that connects perception to actions and their physical consequences, and collecting that data is much more difficult. Robots also have different bodies, sensors, and control interfaces, so sharing experience across them is less straightforward.

There’s also a difference in how we evaluate success. A language model produces an answer; a robot has to act in the physical world, where timing, uncertainty, and recovery matter. Understanding an instruction is only part of the problem. The robot still has to execute it reliably.

So I see these approaches as complementary. Language models can help robots interpret goals and use semantic knowledge, while robotics brings in learning through interaction. We can borrow a lot from the language-model paradigm, but we also need methods that address embodiment and physical control directly.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics foundation models as pursuing a similar broad-training and transfer idea, and says language-model methods can be borrowed. It does not characterize current development as adapting existing large language models.
